10 types of breathing exercises and techniques to try

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we all have those days.
  • When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe.
  • It has been revealed that breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Sources indicate that we all have those days. Your boss just dumped a ton of extra work on your desk, your kids’ school just told you they need to dress up as an ancient Greek philosopher tomorrow, a friend is texting about a personal crisis, and the fridge is empty, so you’ve got to fit in a grocery run. It’s… a lot.

When stress builds up and life feels overwhelming, we often forget to just breathe. But slowing down to focus on your breath can be a simple way to find calm and feel in control again.

It has been revealed that breathing exercises give you tools to manage stress, ease anxiety, and even boost your mood. These breathing techniques are quick to learn and can be done almost anywhere, whether you’re sitting in traffic, lying in bed, or taking a quick break at work.

In this guide, we’ll go through 10 types of breathing exercises, show you how to practice them, and explain how they can help. Here’s where to start.

In a recent development, breathing exercises are simple techniques that help you take control of your breath. When we’re stressed or anxious, our breath usually speeds up, which can actually make us feel more anxious. But doing some focused breathing can help interrupt the cycle in a way that naturally calms your body and mind.

There are lots of techniques, and they each work a little differently or have a particular area of intention. Some breathing exercises are best for reducing anxiety, while others can help improve focus, ease muscle tension, or even prepare you for a good night’s sleep.

Many people use breathing exercises to help in a challenging moment  or simply as part of a regular daily routine to help them keep stress at bay, sleep better, and make it easier to stay calm and focused throughout the day.

Sources indicate that you may be wondering if something so simple can really solve all your problems. And the answer is no —they can’t fill your shopping cart or complete that work project—but they can support your physical and mental health in more ways than one.

Reduces stress and anxiety: Breathing exercises calm the body’s stress response, quieting anxiety and helping you feel more centered.

Improves focus and concentration: Taking a few deep breaths can help sharpen your focus, so you can stay present and engaged.

Sources indicate that helps manage emotions: Focusing on your breath promotes a sense of calm and control, so you can handle emotions better. Struggling with your emotions? Check out these nine emotional regulation tips.

Boosts physical health: Certain breathing exercises can help improve lung capacity, circulation, and even immune response.

Supports better sleep: Breathing exercises like 4–7–8 breathing can help you fall asleep faster and improve the quality of your sleep (these six tips before bed can help too).

Boosts mood and mental wellbeing: Certain techniques, like resonant breathing (which is when you breathe slowly and evenly, usually around 5-6 breaths per minute), can improve your mood and overall sense of wellbeing.

Provides a sense of control: Breathing exercises remind you that even in challenging moments, you have the power to calm yourself.

It has been revealed that when life feels busy or overwhelming, having a variety of breathing exercises in your back pocket can be incredibly helpful. Since each exercise works a bit differently, being familiar with a few means you'll be better able to support yourself in any situation, whether you’re looking to calm down, get focused, or ease into sleep.

As one of the simplest yet most effective ways to calm your body and mind, this technique is especially useful when you need to relieve stress, feel more grounded, or prepare for a restful night’s sleep. If you’re struggling to sleep well, try pairing breathing with these 10 tips to improve your sleep quality.

Recent findings suggest that how to practice: Find a comfortable position, either sitting or lying down. Place one hand on your belly to help you feel each breath as you inhale deeply through your nose, allowing your stomach to rise as you fill your lungs. Hold your breath for a couple of seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, feeling your belly fall. Repeat this pattern for about five to ten breaths, letting your body relax with each exhale.

💙 Learn an easy way to practice deep belly breathing with the Balloon Breath meditation, great for kids and adults!

This type of breathing can help strengthen your diaphragm and improve your body’s ability to take in oxygen. It can be particularly helpful if you're dealing with respiratory issues or you want to ease physical tension (these six tips can also help).

It has been revealed that how to practice: Place one hand on your chest and the other right below your ribs. Breathe in deeply through your nose, aiming to move only your diaphragm (your belly should rise while your chest stays relatively still). Exhale slowly through pursed lips, feeling your belly lower. Practice this for about 5–10 minutes.

A favorite among people who need to manage stress on the go, box breathing helps balance oxygen levels, slow your heart rate, and quickly shift your body into a calm state, making it ideal for high-stress situations.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Visualize a box where each breath segment represents one side. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four as you imagine progressing up the side of the square, hold your breath for another four along the top of the square, exhale for four as you move down the box, then pause for a final count of four to return to the start point. Continue for a few rounds, focusing on maintaining an even rhythm.

Sources indicate that this technique is designed to calm the nervous system and ease anxiety. It’s particularly useful for winding down at the end of the day, so you're feeling ready for sleep. If you’re looking for more sleep support, check out these eight breathing exercises.

It has been revealed that how to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, and hold your breath for a count of seven. Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of eight, aiming for a gentle, complete exhale. Repeat this sequence three to four times, allowing yourself to fully relax.

Alternate nostril breathing can help balance energy, ease stress, and improve focus. It’s a great choice when you’re feeling mentally or physically drained and need a quick reset.

How to practice: Sit in a comfortable position and place your left hand on your knee. With your right thumb, gently close your right nostril and inhale deeply through your left nostril. Close your left nostril with your ring finger, release your right nostril, and exhale fully through the right side. Inhale through the right nostril, close it, then exhale through the left. Continue this alternating pattern 5–10 times.

💙 Let Mel Mah guide you through an alternate nostril breathing practice during the Immune Strength for Optimal Health session.

In a recent development, this technique can increase oxygen flow to the lungs, which can be especially helpful if you have respiratory issues. It’s also calming, so it can ease anxiety and reduce shortness of breath.

How to practice: Breathe in through your nose for a count of two, then purse your lips as if you’re blowing out a candle and exhale slowly for a count of four. Keep the exhale gentle and controlled. Repeat several times, focusing on making the exhale twice as long as the inhale.

The lion’s breath exercise releases tension, particularly in the face and jaw, while also boosting energy and clearing mental fog. It’s an energizing technique that’s great for moments when you feel sluggish or want to improve your mood quickly.

How to practice: Take a deep breath in through your nose. Next, open your mouth wide, stick out your tongue, and forcefully exhale with a loud “ha” sound. Focus on releasing any tension from your face, jaw, and throat. Repeat 3–5 times, letting yourself feel fully present with the exercise.

It has been revealed that also known as coherent breathing, resonant breathing can help calm your nervous system and improve heart rate variability, which is an indicator of how your body adapts to stress and recovers. It’s a great technique for anyone looking to manage stress in the long run.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Breathe in deeply for a count of five and then exhale for a count of five, maintaining a steady, slow rhythm. Aim to take about six breaths per minute, or whatever pace feels comfortable, and focus on keeping your breaths even and controlled.

Sources indicate that use this deeply relaxing technique to reduce frustration and tension. It can be particularly helpful for calming your mind before sleep or during moments of stress.

How to practice: Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and take a deep breath in. As you exhale, make a gentle humming sound, like a bee, and focus on the vibrations in your head and face. Repeat this pattern five to ten times, letting the vibrations soothe your mind.

💙 Practice the humming bee breath in The Daily Move’s Wake Up Your Voice.

Breath counting is a mindful technique that brings you into the present moment, as counting the breaths can quiet racing thoughts and promote relaxation. This helps relieve stress and improve your focus.

Industry observers note that how to practice: Mentally count “one” on the inhale, and then exhale normally. Then count “two” as you breathe to inhale, then silent on the exhale. Keep going all the way up to 10 and then start over again at one. Try this for about 5–10 minutes, focusing on the rhythm of your breathing. If you lose count, start at one again.

💙 Learn to Count the Breaths with guidance from Jeff Warren and The Daily Trip.

It has been revealed that practicing breathing exercises daily is the best way to see results. Even just a few minutes every day can help you feel calmer, more focused, and better able to manage whatever stress comes your way.

Many people find that practicing in the morning helps set a positive tone for the day, while an evening practice can be a great way to unwind and relax before bed, so try both to work out what fits best with your life. And if you’re looking to improve your daily routine, check out these tips to build your morning, workday, and evening routines..

If daily practice feels like too much at first, try starting with just 5–10 minutes a few times a week, as every bit counts toward building a sense of calm and balance.

Breathing exercises can be very helpful for managing anxiety and even calming a panic attack.

When anxiety hits, our breathing often becomes shallow and quick, which can make us feel even more anxious. Practicing slow, deep breathing helps break this cycle, sending a signal to your brain and body that things are okay. Try techniques like deep breathing, box breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing to calm your nervous system during anxious moments.

Recent findings suggest that if you struggle with anxiety or panic attacks, learn breathing techniques in a relaxed setting first. Being familiar with the exercises makes it easier to use them when you’re feeling anxious, so you can start to feel in control and more grounded in tougher times.

Several breathing exercises can be particularly helpful for improving sleep.

Sources indicate that if you’re having trouble sleeping, set aside just a few minutes before bed to practice techniques like 4–7–8 breathing and humming bee breath, as they're known for their calming effects on the nervous system. These exercises can slow down your breathing and heart rate, making it easier to relax and drift off to sleep.

Surprisingly, certain breathing exercises can support your physical fitness and endurance. Techniques like diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, and resonant breathing can improve lung capacity, which can help your body use oxygen more efficiently.

When your lungs are stronger and your breathing is steady, you can perform your favorite sports and exercises better, whether that’s walking, hitting the gym, football, dancing, or any other way you like to get active.

In a recent development, in fact, many pro athletes use breathing techniques to improve their performance and recovery time, so if you want to improve your endurance, try practicing regularly. You can do them either before a workout to warm up your lungs or afterward to help cool down and recover.

When you’re feeling stressed, techniques like box breathing, deep belly breathing, and 4–7–8 breathing can be especially helpful as they’re designed to quickly calm your body and mind.

Box breathing uses equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, and pause, which creates a steady rhythm that helps quiet anxious thoughts.

Deep belly breathing slows your breath and encourages your muscles to relax.

The 4-7-8 technique calms the nervous system in order to calm the stress.

Why Kids with ADHD Get Stuck in the Screen-Time Loop. And How to Break It.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games.
  • Screen addiction is not the problem.
  • Recent findings suggest that once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The adolescent prefrontal cortex is no match for addictive-by-design apps and games. Learn why ADHD brains get hooked on these “other stimulants,” and how to protect them.

Screen addiction is not the problem. Your child is not hooked on their phone, but rather the endless loop of novelty, stimulation, and unpredictable rewards streaming through it. It’s the dopamine; not the device.

Recent findings suggest that once you understand that distinction, you can stop fighting the wrong battle and start winning the right one. Here’s the central point: Phones and video games weren’t as addictive before they got connected to the Internet. A standalone game that you can beat has an ending. A connected game like Fortnite, Roblox, or Minecraft never ends.

For a kid with ADHD, whose brain runs on a dopamine deficit, the Internet is impossible to resist – by design. We hand the most addictive delivery system ever built to the most vulnerable brains, and then ask them to show self-control. That’s not a fair fight.

Recent findings suggest that adolescents and teens with ADHD find screens irresistible, and it’s no wonder why. The ADHD brain is dopamine-deficient, and screens deliver dopamine instantly, reliably, and without effort. Almost everything else in life – school, sports, chores, homework – delivers dopamine slowly, inconsistently, and with lots of effort. The brain always chooses the path of least resistance to its dopamine.

Industry observers note that this isn’t a character flaw or a discipline problem. It’s neurology. The dopamine hit from a connected screen is more powerful and more reinforcing for an ADHD brain than it is for a neurotypical one because the ADHD brain is always hunting for dopamine.

[Download: Managing and Safeguarding Your Child’s Screen Time].

A 2023 meta-analysis of more than 81,000 children found that two or more hours a day of screen time were associated with significantly elevated ADHD risk compared with less than two hours.1 Large longitudinal data from a separate study, which tracked more than 10,000 kids for two years, found that more screen time predicted increased ADHD – and that changes in brain structure helped explain the link.2.

Imaging research has tied greater screen time to altered development in the orbitofrontal cortex, lateral prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex – the regions that govern attention, cognitive control, and reward.

Industry observers note that back in the 1950s, the psychologist B.F. Skinner discovered something the entire tech industry would later weaponize: The most powerful way to drive a behavior isn’t to reward it every time, but to reward it unpredictably. It’s called a variable-ratio reinforcement schedule, and it’s the most addictive reward pattern known to behavioral science.

Industry observers note that it is why slot machines are built as they are. You pull the lever, and you might get nothing, or you might hit the jackpot. Not knowing is what keeps you pulling.

[Read: How Can I Help My Teen Better Manage Screen Time?].

Sources indicate that the same mechanism is now built into the games and apps your child uses every day. The loot box that might contain something rare. The next Roblox round that might go better. The Snapchat notification that might be from someone who matters. The Fortnite match that might end in a Victory Royale. The brain releases dopamine in anticipation of the reward, not when it arrives. This is why your child can’t stop.

Recent findings suggest that but disconnect the device, and the compulsion largely collapses: the variable rewards stop, the social pressure disappears, and the relentless loop finally ends. You don’t have to eliminate every screen, but you must control the connection.

The brain’s prefrontal cortex (the executive function center) isn’t fully developed until around age 25, and perhaps later in an individual with ADHD. Every year you delay access to the Internet is another year of maturity for your child’s executive function system before it’s asked to regulate the most dysregulating product ever made.

Sources indicate that this is why a growing chorus of researchers is now urging parents to delay smartphones until at least high school (around age 14) and social media until at least age 16. The logic is simple: Let the most vulnerable period of brain development happen before your child can access the loop.

Here’s the empowering part: You control the devices, the accounts, the passwords, the router, and the timing of introduction. The strategy below is about exerting that control through environmental design – not nagging, not negotiating, not hoping a dysregulated brain suddenly regulates itself.

Sources indicate that STEP 1: Make a pact. Counter the “I’m the only one without a phone” argument by encouraging three or four other families to agree to delay access together. Ask the parents of your child’s friends to make the pact. It’s easier to hold the line together than alone.

STEP 2: Stop competing with the screen. Control access to the dopamine source through environmental design, not willpower. Screens go in a central location after a certain hour. Devices charge outside bedrooms, every night, no exceptions.

STEP 3: Build “earn-access” systems. Screens become available only after the non-negotiables are done. Homework must be completed, then Xbox. Follow the simple, consistent rules every single day. The structure does the work so you don’t have to problem the reminder.

Michael McLeod is the founder of GrowNOW ADHD and the author of The Executive Function Playbook.

How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving.
  • Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading.
  • My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research indicates that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating upcoming ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

According to recent reports, using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark newly introduced insights. This is particularly crucial because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

Sources indicate that for example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Recent findings suggest that exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Industry observers note that organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is vital, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

According to recent reports, A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as latest research demonstrates—it actually helps it work for you.

Monideepa Tarafdar, Ph.D., is professor of information systems at UMass Amherst.

  • Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.

A study has found that decreasing about 47 grams of sugar intake per day — equivalent to a can of soda — lowers insulin secretion, on average, by 33 percent.

Increasing fibre intake by 5 grams a day — the amount in a half cup of beans — results in a 10 percent reduction of belly fat.

Visceral fat is a type of body fat stored within the abdominal area and internal organs.

This type of fat causes abdominal obesity and is also associated with several health problems, like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.

Dr Emily Ventura and colleagues conducted a 16-week study on overweight Latino adolescents who were between 12 to 19 years old.

They tested if increasing fiber consumption and decreasing sugar intake have an effect on type 2 diabetes risk factors.

“A reduction in visceral fat indicates a reduction in risk for type 2 diabetes, considering that to a greater degree than total body fat, visceral fat [fat surrounding the internal organs] has been shown to be negatively associated with insulin sensitivity.”.

Those who increased fiber intake had a significant reduction in body mass index (-2 percent vs. 2 percent) and visceral adipose tissue (-10 percent vs. no change) compared with those who decreased fiber intake.”.

Being overweight or obese are serious challenges affecting adults and children around the world.

The World Health Organization reports that in 2016 over 1.9 billion adults were overweight and more than 650 million adults were obese.

The authors of this study wrote:.

“Our results suggest that intensive interventions may not be necessary to achieve modifications in sugar and fiber intake.

Accordingly, nutritional guidance given in the primary care or community setting may be sufficient to promote the suggested dietary changes in some individuals.

In addition, policies that promote reduced intake of added sugar and increased intake of fiber could be effective public health strategies for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in this high-risk population.”.

The study was published in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (Ventura et al., 2009).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s how to stir up stronger connections, repair misunderstandings, and nurture relationships.

Sources indicate that time, similarities, vibes, and luck – these are the four core ingredients of friendship. Blended into the mix for adults with ADHD are anxiety, rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD), impulsivity, and social acuity.

The friendship recipe varies by person and circumstance, but the following strategies almost always help.

The challenge: Attention regulation problems may cause you to mentally drift, dominate conversations, or impulsively interrupt.

[Get This Free Download: The ADHD Friendship Guide for Adults].

You’re tracking multiple stimuli simultaneously – body language, tone, word choice, environmental distractions – while managing your own impulses. This requires significantly more energy than most people realize and can result in unintentional social withdrawal.

Use this gauge to monitor your energy levels throughout a social interaction: 10 = Fully charged 4 = Running low; time to recharge 0 = Want to hide under the covers.

You may fear that recharging will damage your relationships, but taking time to rest is the smart choice that allows you to show up as your best self in your relationships.

Recent findings suggest that the dopamine thrill of a upcoming friendship can cause us to text too frequently, share too much too soon, or pressure still-developing friendships. Avoid coming on too strong.

[Read: ADHD and the Social Processing Gap].

Sometimes the challenge isn’t making friends but discerning whether a particular person deserves space in your life.

People pleasing, over-apologizing, overthinking, and shame spirals are signs of RSD.

Amy Kempe, LPC, is the owner of Authentic Life Therapy in Philadelphia.

Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

In a recent development, this eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

Industry observers note that the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

According to recent reports, the unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.

It has been revealed that this week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

Sources indicate that the items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

According to recent reports, the three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

It has been revealed that the five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

#206544. How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3396 w)

How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone.
  • Developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind. But here’s the truth: self-love isn’t something you’re born knowing how to do. It’s something you learn. And like any meaningful practice, it takes time, intention, and a lot of patience.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone. Many of us were never taught how to speak to ourselves with compassion, how to set boundaries that honor our needs, or how to practice everyday self-respect. That’s where this guide comes in—because it’s never too late to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered. It means learning to treat yourself the way you’d treat someone you care deeply about—with gentleness, understanding, and care. Whether you’re struggling with self-worth, navigating difficult emotions, or simply trying to reconnect with the real you, these seven steps offer a foundation for how to practice self-love in real, actionable ways.

Recent findings suggest that from building self-awareness and setting healthy boundaries to practicing forgiveness and celebrating your wins, this guide is here to support your growth. Start small, stay consistent, and trust that loving yourself is not only possible—it’s one of the most empowering things you’ll ever do.

Self-love is exactly how it sounds—it’s a love for yourself and having an interest in your own well-being and happiness. Loving yourself doesn’t mean being self-centered or selfish. It’s about forming a caring relationship with yourself, like getting to know a good friend.

Sources indicate that the idea of loving yourself isn’t just a ‘feel-good’ concept—it’s essential for mental health. Research highlights that self-compassion is linked to lower stress, reduced anxiety, and even improved physical health. People who actively practice self-love tend to set better boundaries, build stronger relationships, and experience less burnout.

Self-love is crucial because the relationship you have with yourself sets the tone for how you deal with every aspect of life: your bonds with others, the way you handle challenges, and how you celebrate joys. When you’re kind and understanding toward yourself, you’re better equipped to navigate life’s ups and downs.

But how do you start loving yourself? Where do you even begin? Self-love starts with understanding where you stand right now. Take a look at your current feelings toward your mental health, motivation, and overall well-being. Are you harsh with yourself when things don’t go as planned? Do you forget to celebrate your wins, especially the small ones? These little check-ins can pave the path to walking toward self-love.

Recent findings suggest that loving yourself isn’t a switch you turn on or off. It’s a practice that takes time, commitment, and, well, practice, to cultivate. For many of us, the idea of loving ourselves feels out of reach. That’s why it’s often helpful to break the concept of self-love down into its distinctive elements — including self-trust, self-compassion, and self-awareness.

Sources indicate that this can make it easier to start developing a self-love practice that feels achievable and manageable. So instead of viewing self-love as something you have to win at, try practicing these seven steps.

Self-awareness: Understand your feelings, thoughts, and behaviors.

Self-expression: Be true to who you are in all areas of life.

Self-care: Take care of your body and mind.

Self-trust: Believe in your ability to handle life’s ups and downs.

Self-compassion: Be kind to yourself, especially when times are tough.

Self-respect: Honor your worth by setting healthy boundaries.

According to recent reports, self-acceptance: Embrace who you are, including the parts you don’t find perfect. Remember what we said about perfection?

Recent findings suggest that sometimes practicing self-love means taking action or establishing boundaries to protect your mental health. Here are a few IRL examples of how you can practice self-love today.

Prioritize rest to recharge: Imagine you’ve had a long week, and instead of squeezing in one more task, you decide to turn off your devices and enjoy a full night’s sleep. Studies have shown that adequate rest improves mood, cognitive function, and emotional resilience​. By honoring your body’s need for recovery, you demonstrate that you value your well-being above productivity.

Say no to unhealthy relationships: Picture being invited to a gathering where you know that certain individuals drain your energy. Choosing to decline isn't selfish; it’s self-preservation. Healthy boundaries are key to having self-respect and healthy relationships. Saying no clears space for connections that truly nourish you​.

According to recent reports, practice forgiveness for yourself: Maybe you’ve made a mistake at work and feel embarrassed. Instead of spiraling into self-criticism, try acknowledging the error, learning from it, and moving on. Self-compassion may help reduce anxiety and create more resilience, helping you recover more effectively from setbacks​. Mistakes are normal, and it’s all about “failing up”.

Create moments of mindfulness amid the chaos: Let’s say your day is hectic, and stress feels overwhelming. This is the moment to pause for a brief grounding exercise (here’s one of our favorites). Maybe you focus on your breath or tune into your surroundings. These types of practice not only calm your nervous system but also remind you of your ability to care for yourself even in small, meaningful ways​.

According to recent reports, treat yourself with the same kindness you show others: When you reflect on a recent accomplishment—massive or small—you choose to celebrate it instead of brushing it off. There are huge benefits to recognizing your personal achievements. Giving yourself a pat on the back may help boost self-esteem and even long-term happiness​.

Self-love can feel unfamiliar and challenging to some of us, particularly if we’ve got into a habit of being hard on ourselves. The steps above can help break down the idea of self-love into more manageable elements.

Recent findings suggest that but what practical things can we do to cultivate practices like self-awareness and self-trust? We got you. For each of the self-love steps, we’re sharing tools, techniques and exercises you can use to help get you closer to loving yourself.

Industry observers note that building self-awareness helps cultivate self-love by giving you further insight into what makes you who you are on an emotional level. Begin by tuning into your thoughts and feelings.

What makes you feel happy, sad, or excited? Then, take it a step further. What makes you feel overwhelmed, overjoyed, or anxious? Knowing yourself is the first step to loving yourself.

Practice mindfulness: Try mindfulness practices to stay present and understand your thoughts and feelings better.

Educate yourself: Empower yourself through education by reading books, attending workshops, or engaging in discussions that promote self-awareness, self-compassion, and self-love.

Recent findings suggest that schedule regular self-check-ins: Reflect on your feelings, goals, and progress. Write them down, and revisit them often.

Tune into yourself through meditation: Spend some quiet time meditating to help declutter your mind and tap into your desires.

Sources indicate that let go of what no longer serves you: Let go of old habits or relationships that no longer contribute to your growth or happiness. We know this practice can be difficult, but removing what no longer brings you joy makes space for the good to come in.

💙 If you want to learn to relate to your thoughts in a healthier way, press play on Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty.

Loving yourself also means giving yourself permission to express your thoughts and feelings both inwardly and outwardly. Express yourself honestly in your day-to-day life. Be true to who you are, whether you’re simply chatting with friends or making significant decisions at work.

Engage in creative expression: Whether it's drawing, writing, or any other form of creative expression, allowing your creativity to flow freely can become an act of self-love.

Sources indicate that discover newly introduced hobbies: Explore new activities that bring you joy and allow you to express yourself. Have you always wanted to try your hand at a group sport or acting? Now’s the time to try.

It has been revealed that journaling: Write down your thoughts, feelings, and experiences daily, and don’t hold back. Expressing yourself through writing can be cathartic and a helpful step in falling back in love with who you are.

In a recent development, spend quality time with yourself: Enjoy your own tech giant by doing things that make you happy. There’s a difference between doing something alone and feeling lonely. Embracing solo time and solo outings to the movies, dinner, or even a cooking class can be empowering, and, believe it or not, ridiculously fun!

According to recent reports, 💙 Journaling can be a great way to process feelings and encourage self-love. Check out our five Calm Journals plus our Feelings Wheel to get you started.

Caring for your body and mind plays a major role in cultivating self-love. Simple acts like mindful eating, exercise, and making time to relax can make a big difference in your overall well-being.

Take breaks when you need them: Remember to rest — even a micro-break can refresh and rejuvenate you. Want to amp up your rest break a notch? Take it outside. Being in nature can naturally calm and refresh your mind and body.

Practice relaxation: Use techniques like deep breathing or yoga to relax your body and focus on your breath.

Nourish your body: Fuel your body with nourishing food that makes you feel good.

Prioritize sleep: Ensure you get enough good-quality sleep—it’s crucial for your well-being.

Connect with your body through movement: Move your body in a way that feels good for you. It could be dancing in your apartment to your favorite album, walking outside, or stretching from the comfort of your bed.

Ask for support when you need it: Reach out for help when you need it. Asking for support is a sign of strength.

💙 Move your body with some Mindful Movement thanks to the Daily Move.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to love yourself if you don’t trust yourself. Embracing self-trust is about understanding that you have the ability to make the correct decisions for your life. Even when things don’t go as planned, believing that you can learn and grow from the experience is an notable step in building self-trust.

Set realistic expectations: Set achievable goals to build your sense of accomplishment and reinforce the belief you have in yourself to overcome.

In a recent development, practice patience: Be patient with yourself as you uncover what self-love means to you. Trusting yourself takes time. Let it.

Monitor your negative self-talk: Pay attention to how you talk to yourself. Are you harsh or unforgiving? Do you speak about yourself poorly? Take note of how you speak to yourself and work to make it more positive and encouraging.

In a recent development, make a list of things you’re proud of: Reflect on your achievements and the things that make you proud. Look back on them when you need a dose of inspiration, and remind yourself and believe that you can make yourself proud again and again.

💙 Check out our 7 Days of Self-Esteem series to build your self-acceptance and boost your inner strength.

In a recent development, be kind to yourself. Always. Especially when life gets tough. Celebrate your wins, learn from life’s mishaps, and don’t be too hard on yourself when it all doesn’t go as planned. Having compassion for self means you deeply care about your well-being. And feelings of deep care often mean love.

Practice positive affirmations: Craft and repeat positive phrases daily to help drive away those pesky negative thoughts.

It has been revealed that develop a self-forgiveness practice: Forgive yourself for past mistakes or perceived shortcomings. You’re only human. Remember that.

Try a loving-kindness meditation: Practice loving-kindness meditation to cultivate love and kindness toward yourself and others.

Put your hand over your heart and breathe deeply: This simple gesture can bring comfort and a sense of self-compassion.

💙 Try Loving-Kindness Meditation as a guided practice with Tamara Levitt.

Respect yourself by setting boundaries to show yourself—and others—that your desires, wants, and needs matter. When we respect our boundaries and our wants, we’re showing ourselves love by prioritizing our needs.

Seek supportive communities: Surround yourself with supportive, loving, and understanding people who uplift you. The more you’re around people you respect and admire, the more you might begin to respect, admire, and love yourself.

According to recent reports, set boundaries: Give yourself permission to say no to things or people that drain your energy. Setting boundaries and sticking to them is an act of self-love, as it showcases to the world around you that you give yourself what you want and need.

In a recent development, volunteer: Engage in volunteer work to connect with a sense of purpose and community. Volunteer to walk dogs at a local animal shelter or serve meals at a community kitchen. Giving back brings a deep sense of purpose and gratitude, and a way to give yourself love is to give love to others in need.

It has been revealed that celebrate your progress and success: Celebrate your wins, major or small, as all victories are steps toward growth. You’d cheer for a friend’s achievement, regardless of its size, wouldn’t you? Show yourself the same love and kindness and become your own cheerleader.

Honor your commitments to yourself: When you make a promise to yourself, keep it. Honoring your promises to yourself can help to build self-respect, which, as we’ve learned, enhances self-love by showing yourself that you’re a priority.

💙 Learn even more about self-love with our Relationship with Self series.

Sources indicate that embrace yourself wholeheartedly. Every single inch. Even the parts you’d like to improve upon. You have nothing to gain by being hard on yourself, and everything to gain by being loving and accepting of yourself as you move along on your path in life.

Recent findings suggest that when you accept yourself, you’re declaring the love you have for yourself, regardless of what happens. Think of self-acceptance as a loving embrace.

Learn to laugh with yourself: Embracing a light-hearted approach toward life and how you view yourself can help you meet those challenging moments with more ease and less friction.

Embrace where you are now: Appreciate the present moment. You’re here now. So, be here now and try to enjoy the journey.

Make space for your emotions: Allow yourself to feel your emotions. Emotions are natural, but ignoring them can become detrimental to your well-being.

It has been revealed that drop the comparison: Avoid comparing yourself to others. You’re unique and have your own journey.

Practice gratitude: Cultivate gratitude by acknowledging the qualities you appreciate about yourself and your life. This can shift your focus from what's lacking to what's abundant.

💙 If you’re looking to build a daily gratitude practice, check out the 7 Days of Gratitude.

In a recent development, morning affirmations: Start your day with one self-loving statement (e.g., "I am enough"). This may reduce stress and boost confidence.

Set small self-care goals: Even five minutes of journaling or stretching may shift your mindset toward self-love.

Mirror work: Look in the mirror and say something kind about yourself. It might feel awkward at first, but it may build self-acceptance.

Limit self-criticism: Notice when you’re being hard on yourself. Pause and reframe it as if you were talking to a friend.

It has been revealed that practice gratitude: Write down three things you appreciate about yourself daily. Gratitude is potentially linked to higher self-worth.

Self-love is essential in relationships because it provides the foundation for healthy, balanced, and meaningful connections. When you love yourself, you develop confidence and emotional stability, which allows you to communicate your needs and feelings openly without fear of judgment. This clarity helps you to form stronger communications and can also reduce misunderstandings. Self-love also empowers you to set and maintain healthy boundaries, ensuring that your relationships are built on mutual respect rather than people-pleasing or overextending yourself. (Learn how to stop being a people pleaser with these 10 tips.).

According to recent reports, when you feel secure in your own worth, you can offer love freely without expecting others to validate you, and you’re better equipped to accept care from others because you believe you deserve it. Ultimately, self-love nurtures healthier, more fulfilling connections by allowing you to show up as your best self, while also creating space for others to do the same.

Starting on the path of self-love begins with self-awareness. Notice your thoughts, feelings and actions. Begin to recognize what makes you smile or what makes you feel uneasy. Once you have a better understanding of yourself, you can start taking steps toward treating yourself with more kindness and respect. Remember, it's a journey—there are no deadlines, and you don’t have to rush. And if you ever feel lost, you can always revisit the seven steps to gently reintroduce self-love practices.

It has been revealed that if you're struggling to love yourself, start by identifying the thoughts that hold you back. Are you constantly comparing yourself to others? Do you feel unworthy of kindness? Self-love begins with self-awareness. Explore these steps to start loving yourself today:.

Shift your internal dialogue: Notice when you're being self-critical and replace it with a more compassionate thought.

Prioritize self-care: Even small acts like deep breathing or a 10-minute walk can reinforce your self-worth.

Surround yourself with positivity: Reduce exposure to toxic relationships or social media comparisons.

Celebrate small wins: Even recognizing personal growth (no matter how small) strengthens self-love.

In a recent development, struggling with self-love is a common human experience, so you're not alone. Sometimes, past experiences, societal expectations, or harsh self-judgment can create blocks on the path to self-love. It's notable to remember that overcoming these hurdles takes time and practice, but with patience and persistence, it can get easier. Engaging in self-compassion practices and seeking support when needed are great steps when you encounter these struggles.

Industry observers note that lack of self-love can show up in different ways. It could be in the form of constant self-criticism, ignoring your own needs, or having difficulty with accepting compliments. It might also appear as feeling undeserving of positive experiences or neglecting self-care. The good news is that recognizing these signs is the first step toward change. Once you see them, you can start taking steps to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Self-love habits are small, daily actions that nurture a loving relationship with yourself. They could be as simple as speaking kindly to yourself, taking breaks when needed, or engaging in activities that make you happy. Other self-love habits include practicing gratitude, spending time in nature, eating nourishing food, and exercising in a way that feels good to your body. The goal is to create habits that make you feel loved, respected, and cared for.

According to recent reports, loving yourself isn’t a switch you flip—it’s a process. If self-love feels out of reach, start small. Acknowledge your feelings without judgment, challenge negative self-talk, and practice one self-kindness daily. Maybe it’s treating yourself with the same patience you’d give a friend, or simply recognizing that you deserve happiness.

One simple trick is to ask yourself, “If my best friend was feeling this way, what would I tell them?”.

Sources indicate that often, we extend kindness to others more easily than to ourselves. Flip that perspective inward.

The first step in learning how to love yourself is awareness—tuning into your thoughts, noticing how you speak to yourself, and identifying patterns of self-criticism. Once you're aware of your inner dialogue, you can begin to shift it with self-kindness, small acts of self-care, and daily affirmations. Remember: every loving thought counts.

The meaning of self love is caring for yourself emotionally, physically, and mentally with the same compassion you’d offer someone you love. It means honoring your needs, setting boundaries, and treating yourself with kindness—not just when things are going well, but especially when they aren’t.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with vitamin B12 deficiency were three times more likely to be suffering this problem.
  • People with vitamin B12 deficiency were three times more likely to be suffering this problem.
  • Feeling depressed can be a sign of vitamin B12 deficiency, a study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with vitamin B12 deficiency were three times more likely to be suffering this problem.

People with vitamin B12 deficiency were three times more likely to be suffering this problem.

Feeling depressed can be a sign of vitamin B12 deficiency, a study finds.

People with a vitamin B12 deficiency are three times more likely to be experiencing ‘melancholic’ depression.

Melancholic depression mostly involves depressed mood.

Some of the other most common symptoms of depression are decreased interest in life or pleasure, energy loss and concentration problems.

The study also found a link between low folate intake and depression.

Folates include vitamin B9, folacin and folic acid.

People with a low intake of folates were 50 percent more likely to be experiencing melancholic depression.

The research included 2,806 Finnish people whose nutritional status and depression symptoms were assessed.

Although vitamin B12 and folates were linked to melancholic depression, the same link was not seen with non-melancholic depression.

Symptoms of non-melancholic depression cluster around anxiety and low self-esteem, with less emphasis on depressed mood.

Dr Jussi Seppälä, the study’s first author, said:.

“The findings have practical implications in the care of patients with depressive symptoms.

For example, it may be wise to avoid medication causing weight gain among patients with non-melancholic depression, whereas melancholic depressive symptoms may call for a closer look at the quality of the patient’s diet.”.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is easy to rectify with supplements or by dietary changes.

The body uses vitamin B12 to make red blood cells and to keep the nervous system healthy.

Other common signs of vitamin B12 deficiency include experiencing muscle weakness and being constipated.

Meanwhile, some of the best dietary sources of folates include:.

Folate levels are particularly high in chickpeas, yeast extract, lentils and broad beans.

The study was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders (Seppälä et al., 2012).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

ADHD Medications May Improve Brain Fog in Perimenopausal Women: Fresh Research

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Preliminary evidence highlights self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.
  • In a recent development, stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego.
  • During the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Preliminary evidence highlights self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.

In a recent development, stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego. (These findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.)1.

During the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD? Executive Dysfunction in Perimenopause: A Scoping Review of the Role of ADHD Medications,” researchers discussed the effectiveness of two ADHD medications: lisdexamphetamine (brand name: Vyvanse), a stimulant, and atomoxetine, a non-stimulant. They studied the impact of these medications on cognition and ADHD symptom severity in women aged 45 to 60 years during the perimenopausal period. The systematic review included three crossover randomized controlled trials involving 60 patients and two cross-sectional studies of 6,048 patients from Iceland and the U.K.

The study found that both lisdexamphetamine (LDX) and atomoxetine (ATX) significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction, as measured by the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, compared to placebo. The BADDS scores for LDX people dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared to 29.8 with placebo. The BADDS scores for ATX users fell from 38.6 to 25.5, compared to 30.1 with placebo. Neuroimaging data from a subset of women taking LDX further supports these findings.

During perimenopause, declining or fluctuating estrogen levels affect dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. As a result, many perimenopausal women experience “brain fog,” which is an umbrella term for forgetfulness, slow thinking, difficulty finding words, and reduced concentration, which can also be a symptom of ADHD. This overlap often leaves clinicians trying to discern whether a patient’s brain fog stems from hormonal fluctuations or undiagnosed ADHD, or both.

“Many women at perimenopause notice changes in focus, memory, and organization that look a lot like ADHD, and the two can be hard to tell apart,” said lead author Jennifer Tat, M.D. candidate and fourth-year medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

In an ADDitude survey of more than 5,000 women with diagnosed and undiagnosed ADHD, 94% of survey respondents stated their ADHD symptoms grew more severe during perimenopause and menopause. During this stage, respondents said the most impactful ADHD symptoms were brain fog or memory issues, and overwhelm, both of which 70% of women said had a “life-altering impact” in their 40s and 50s.

In a recent development, “Brain fog became unmanageable,” wrote one 45-year-old mother of two who entered perimenopause at age 41. “Distractibility increased and my inability to complete work tasks in an appropriate amount of time decreased. I began spending all night working just to keep up. Things that I used to have unconscious strategies to deal with were no longer manageable.”.

“I never experienced rage or brain fog before perimenopause,” wrote one woman. “Overwhelm has been more frequent in recent years, and depression began in my 40s. I definitely attribute some of this to hormonal changes.”.

Sources indicate that “In perimenopause, the brain fog and memory, inattention, distractibility, perfectionism, hyperactivity, and restlessness challenges become progressively worse,” wrote a 52-year-old woman diagnosed with ADHD at age 50. “I have always had these symptoms, but I was able to manage them with systems that I created for myself. My ability to manage them has declined significantly, and this makes these symptoms seem like they are the worst they have ever been.”.

While preliminary evidence from the systematic review found ADHD medications improve subjective executive function, the medications had little to no significant impact on objective cognitive measures, according to tests measuring working memory and sustained attention.

Prior research suggests otherwise.

According to recent reports, in the ADDitude article “Could ADHD Medications Improve Memory, Focus & Organization in Menopausal Women? The Research Says Yes,” the late Thomas E. Brown, Ph.D., described how his research with C. Neill Epperson, M.D., found ADHD medications alleviated cognitive problems resembling ADHD symptoms in menopausal women without ADHD.

The series of three studies measured symptoms with BADDS, which Brown developed. The first study found that ATX treatment significantly improved BADDS scores for working memory; focus scores improved in BADDS scores for women treated with ATX.2 In the second study, executive functions improved, including an objective measure of short-term working memory, in 41% of menopausal women taking 20 to 60 mg LDX daily, compared to 17% for the women on the placebo.3 The third study examined the effects of LDX on the brain functioning of women with no history of ADHD, but with reported cognitive difficulties with working memory, organization, focus, and attention that had begun during menopause.4.

According to recent reports, “As predicted, neuroimaging data showed that LDX activated executive networks in specific areas of the brain,” Brown wrote. “Those data also showed that LDX’s effect on specific brain regions was associated with improved BADDS scores overall, and with BADDS scores for activation and alertness/effort. Imaging data indicated that improvements in brain activation were significantly larger when women were on LDX than when they were on placebo.”.

The studies were published in peer-reviewed medical journals in 2011, 2015, and 2017; however, Brown wrote in 2021, “results of that research have not yet been widely recognized.”.

There is right now no FDA-approved pharmacological intervention for executive dysfunction and brain fog during perimenopause or menopause. Research on the most effective treatments for ADHD during perimenopause is limited as well. That said, Patricia Quinn, M.D., explained during a 2026 ADDitude webinar that available data and observational evidence suggest that many women could benefit from estrogen supplementation and increased stimulant dosages during this phase.

“Perimenopause is when you need the most help, the most support,” Quinn stated in her webinar, “Perimenopause in Women with ADHD.” “Estrogen… makes your stimulant more effective.”.

One roadblock to care is the fact that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate menopause, according to a study published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health. The 2026 study cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”5.

Combined, these preliminary findings could open the door to a nonhormone therapeutic option for addressing perimenopausal executive dysfunction, according to researcher Tat.

In a recent development, “Our review found early signs that ADHD medications may help women feel more on top of their daily lives,” Tat stated. “While it’s too early to recommend these medications, a quick screen for ADHD symptoms is a simple step that could help women get the right care.”.
