Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food.
  • According to recent reports, news spreads like wildfire across the camp.
  • Recent findings suggest that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help.

According to recent reports, news spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

Recent findings suggest that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

It has been revealed that insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender, war, and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical.

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

Recent findings suggest that anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth, and social status. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

Recent findings suggest that most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy, inequality only spread with the development of agriculture, and humans are noble by nature.

In a recent development, some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, The Dawn of Everything, calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth.

So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.

In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

It has been revealed that like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold, and hoarded ritual knowledge. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans.

Gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men, and give more respect to better hunters. Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting, and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision making.

No society lacks informal leadership. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives.

In a recent development, our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status, and autonomy.

A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving, often through strongly stated demands or complaints.

Industry observers note that another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community.

Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

Ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata.

Like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

Egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.

Breaking: 25 unique experience gift ideas for everyone on your list

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.
  • It has been revealed that when life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.

It has been revealed that when life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat. A coffee date, a class you could take together, or a simple invitation to step away from your routine for a few hours. Gifting experiences is becoming more common as people increasingly value things to do rather than things to have. Experiences create memories, prolonged joy, and ways to connect and bond with your loved ones.

Let’s explore why this trend is becoming a thoughtful option for many, and how to choose the right option for the people in your life.

It has been revealed that gifting an experience means offering someone the chance to do or enjoy something, rather than giving them a physical item. It could be a short outing, a shared class, a small adventure, or even a moment of relaxation. The focus is on creating a meaningful interaction or memory.

At its core, an experience gift acknowledges who someone is and what matters to them — comfort, curiosity, connection, or rest. It’s a way of saying, I see what brings you joy or ease, and building a shared experience around that. This can feel especially supportive for people whose lives are busy or emotionally stretched.

Because these gifts are flexible, they work across relationships and budgets. They can be shared or solo, active or restful, planned or open-ended. They offer a moment that feels nourishing and special for someone you care about.

💙 If relaxation is what they need, a Calm gift card gives them access to sleep support, meditation, and stress tools.

While research on experience gifting is still growing, studies highlight how shared time and supportive interactions can strengthen relationships and help people feel more connected.

And for the giver, choosing an experience can relieve some of the pressure to pick the “perfect” item. Plus, you get to be a bit more creative since experiences can be catered to the person in question more accurately than a newly introduced sweater or scented bath salts.

Sources indicate that these gifts also tend to linger in memory. A walk through a upcoming neighborhood, a class where you learned something together, or an afternoon spent doing something familiar but intentional can shape how people feel long after the moment ends. The emotional takeaway is often stronger than anything wrapped.

Choosing an experience gift doesn’t need to feel complicated. A few gentle questions can help you find something that feels both thoughtful and doable:.

What feels realistic for them right now?

What genuinely matches their interests?

Will this support connection in a way that feels natural?

These considerations keep the focus on care rather than wow-factor. The most memorable experience gifts are often the ones that feel easy to say yes to.

Industry observers note that related read: What is the receiving gifts love language? Plus, 10 examples.

Experience gifts don’t have to be substantial, expensive, or Instagram-ready. The most meaningful ones usually feel simple, personal, and easy to follow through on. Below are ideas for different people in your life, with concrete examples and small tweaks to make each one feel low-pressure yet purposeful.

Sources indicate that 1. Slow morning together: Gift a “no-alarm morning” where you initiative nothing except being together. This could look like making breakfast at home, wandering to a café, or staying in pajamas with a movie. You can write it as a simple coupon: “One slow morning: no chores, no plans, just us.” This works well for tired partners who crave rest more than busy plans.

Sources indicate that 2. A shared learning experience: Choose a class or workshop that feels fun. Cooking, pottery, a dance class, a cocktail-making session, or even a virtual class from home. The goal is to play, not create a fresh skill. Pick a time that fits your usual schedule, and make it clear there’s no pressure to be good at it. You’re just trying it out.

3. A “memory lane” date: Revisit places that matter to your relationship: where you met, a favorite early date spot, or a park you love. You can build a simple route and add tiny prompts, like sharing a favorite memory at each stop. This turns a regular outing into something personal without costing much.

4. At-home retreat night: Create a mini retreat without leaving the house. That might mean takeout, candles, phones off for a few hours, and a shared activity like a puzzle, show, or playlist swap. You can include options on a card so they can choose: a massage, a movie, a board game, or just some quiet time together.

Sources indicate that 5. Surprise “care afternoon”: Block off a few hours for them where you take on a task they’ve been dreading—organizing a small space, handling an errand, or taking something off their mental load—and then follow it with something relaxing, like a walk or coffee. The experience is both practical support and quality time.

6. Future adventure fund: If money is tight or schedules are messy, create a “future adventure” envelope. Add a small amount of money, a short list of possible outings (day trip, concert, special restaurant), and a promise to choose an option together when life settles a bit. The gift is the intention and shared planning, not just the event itself.

💙 Explore 5 Steps to Stronger Relationships with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Related read: How to build emotional connection in relationships.

1. Family game or movie night: Strategy a night with a few easy games or a movie everyone can enjoy. Add snacks, cozy blankets, and a pause on chores for a few hours. You can give the night a “ticket” and let family members vote on the game or film. Keep it simple so no one has to host a perfect event.

2. Seasonal outing: Choose something tied to the time of year: apple picking, a beach afternoon, a holiday light walk, or a picnic in the park. The key is to keep expectations reasonable. Pick something close by, flexible with the weather, and not too long. Add a warm drink stop or simple treat to make it feel special.

3. Family photo walk: Go for a walk through a neighborhood, park, or favorite spot and take casual photos of each other and everyday moments. This isn’t about staged portraits. It’s about capturing small, real pieces of your life together. Later, you can print a few favorites as a follow-up surprise.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Shared creative project: Start something you can all contribute to: a family recipe book, a small garden, a scrapbook, or a shared playlist for car rides. The “gift” is the first session to begin the project, plus a initiative to keep it going at a relaxed pace.

5. Story or memory night: For older family members, gift a relaxed evening where you ask about their stories — childhood, early jobs, favorite memories. You can record audio or write things down if they’re comfortable. This can feel especially meaningful for grandparents or relatives who don’t often get to share their history.

6. Chore-free experience swap: Offer to trade time: you handle childcare, yard work, or a big errand so another family member can enjoy their own experience like a class, a nap, a solo walk, or quiet time at a café. The experience you’re gifting is space and freedom, which many busy adults crave more than objects.

💙 Family life feels overwhelming? Check out the Ease Parenting Stress series with Jeff Warren on the Calm app.

Related read: Here's why you should establish family values (and how to do it).

1. Friendship field trip: Pick a spot you’ve both wanted to visit, maybe a new café, nearby town, market, bookstore, or trail. Make it simple: transportation, one planned stop, and room to wander. You can name it something fun on the card, like “Field Trip Day: You + Me + Snacks.”.

According to recent reports, 2. Theme night at home: Instead of going out, bring the theme to your living room. Taco night, cozy soup night, DIY spa night, or favorite childhood snacks night. The gift is that you plan the details so your friend just highlights up and relaxes. This works well for introverts or friends on a budget.

In a recent development, 3. Shared creative time: Gift a “creative hang” where you both bring whatever you want to work on like, drawing, writing, knitting, music, or even organizing photos. Add music, snacks, and low-pressure conversation. For friends who feel guilty about not making time for hobbies, this can feel like a gentle permission slip.

Industry observers note that 4. Local class or workshop together: Check out low-stakes options like pottery, candle making, painting, or a casual fitness class. Pick something that doesn’t require special gear or skills and frame it as an experiment, not a performance: “We’ll probably be bad at this, and that’s half the fun.”.

It has been revealed that 5. Walk-and-talk ritual: Offer a series of scheduled or flexible walk-and-talks. Maybe once a month, every other week, or whenever you both can manage. The experience is regular emotional check-ins built into movement and fresh air. If walking isn’t accessible, this can be a sit-and-sip ritual at a park or café.

💙 Learn more about Meaningful Practice for Meaningful Friendship on the Calm app.

Related read: How to be a better friend: 7 tips to improve your relationships.

It has been revealed that 1. One-on-one “date” with you: Strategy a simple outing centered around their interests like ice cream, a playground, a comic shop, the library, or a favorite café. The notable part is your undivided attention — no multitasking, no rushing. You can make a small “VIP pass” with their name and the activity.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Activity day pass: Gift a trip to a kid-friendly place: zoo, aquarium, children’s museum, climbing gym, trampoline park, or mini golf. To keep expectations realistic, include what’s covered (entry, one snack) and how long you’ll stay. That clarity helps avoid meltdowns.

Industry observers note that 4. Backyard or park adventure: Create a small “explorer kit” experience. Maybe that’s a printed map, a simple scavenger hunt, or nature bingo. Then take them to a nearby park or backyard to complete it together. The kit can be as simple as a folded paper with things to look for: birds, leaves, colors, shapes.

5. Choose-your-own-activity coupon book: Instead of one big outing, make a few small coupons they can redeem over time: “Stay up 30 minutes late,” “Pick tonight’s dinner,” “Board game together,” “Extra story at bedtime.” This spreads the experience out and gives them a sense of choice.

Sources indicate that 6. Screen-time with purpose: If screens are part of your life (for most families, they are), turn it into an intentional experience. A planned movie night with popcorn and cozy blankets, or a co-op video game session where you play alongside them. The shift is from “background screen” to “shared screen time.”.

7. Skill-building mini lesson: Offer to teach them something they’ve shown interest in, like basic cooking, drawing, sewing, photography, or music. Keep it short and fun — 30 to 60 minutes with lots of breaks. The experience is meant to help them feel capable and supported, not pushed to master something.

Related read: 61 fun and simple mindfulness activities for kids to enjoy.

According to recent reports, good experience gifts feel easy to enjoy and don’t add pressure. Simple outings like a coffee date, museum visit, or nature walk work well, as do classes or small day trips.

If you’re unsure, think about what the person already loves—quiet spaces, creativity, movement, or social time—and choose something that gently supports those interests.

Industry observers note that budget-friendly experience gifts often center on time or support rather than cost. A homemade coupon for help with errands, a movie night at home, or a walk together can feel more meaningful than anything store-bought.

You can also offer a few options, like a baked treat, a playlist walk, or a shared hour of connection, so the gift feels personal without being expensive.

Experience gifts ease the pressure of traditional gifting and help strengthen connections. They don’t create clutter and often require less guesswork than choosing an item.

According to recent reports, because they create memories, they can feel more lasting and emotionally meaningful. Early research also suggests shared time and supportive interactions may help people feel more connected.

It has been revealed that examples include classes, tours, local events, shared meals, creative workshops, or simple nature outings. They can also be quieter moments like helping with a task or planning a cozy night in.

According to recent reports, even small gestures—like sharing a playlist—count. The impact comes from the feeling the experience creates, not the size of the activity.

In a recent development, if you’re unsure, offer a few choices rather than picking one activity. Options like a coffee outing, nature walk, or game night let the person choose what fits their energy. A flexible gift card to a café, movie theater, or class platform also works. Choice keeps the gift from feeling like an obligation.

It has been revealed that families often enjoy simple, low-pressure activities that include everyone. Seasonal outings, game nights, and local events work well because they’re easy to plan.

In a recent development, shared projects—like cooking or gardening—or gifts of time, such as taking on chores so someone can rest, can also be meaningful. The best family gifts support connection without adding stress.

Friends tend to appreciate experiences that feel connecting and relaxed. This might be a field trip to a latest café, a creative class, a cozy night in, or a shared walk.

According to recent reports, some friends enjoy active outings, while others prefer crafting or volunteering together. The goal is to match their energy and make time together feel restorative.

Experience gifts can feel better for some people because they avoid clutter, reduce pressure, and often feel more meaningful. They shift the focus toward presence and memory-making rather than buying things.

While not everyone prefers experiences, they offer a gentle alternative for people who value connection or feel overwhelmed by physical items.

12 common physical symptoms of anxiety (and how to ease them)

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain. Sometimes the first sign is your heart pounding for no clear reason, or a wave of nausea before a significant conversation. You might feel dizzy, short of breath, or like there’s a knot in your stomach. You’re not in immediate danger, but your body is reacting as if you are.

This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like. They can be alarming, especially if you don’t recognize them as anxiety right away. But your body responds this way for a reason, and understanding it can take some of the fear out of the experience.

Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.

Anxiety can affect your body before you've consciously registered that you're anxious at all. These are among the most common physical symptoms.

1. Racing or pounding heart (palpitations): A fast-beating or fluttering heart is one of the most recognized signs of anxiety. When your body senses a threat, it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart rate to pump blood to your muscles faster. This is useful when you actually need to run. Less so when you’re just checking your inbox.

In a recent development, 2. Shortness of breath: Anxiety can make you feel like you can’t get a full breath, or like you’re slightly suffocating. Anxious breathing tends to be shallow and fast, which can lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can feel scary, and anxiety is a common cause.

3. Chest tightness or pain: Muscle tension is a core part of the anxiety response and can be most noticeable in your chest, where you might feel tightness, pressure, or even mild pain. Seek emergency care if you feel sudden or severe chest pain, pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw.

Sources indicate that 4. Dizziness or lightheadedness: Fast, shallow breathing can also leave you feeling faint or spaced out.

According to recent reports, 5. Tingling or numbness: Lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood can affect nerve signals and cause tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in the hands, feet, or face. It can feel unsettling, but it’s usually short-lived. Numbness on one side of the body, sudden weakness, or trouble speaking needs urgent care.

In a recent development, 6. Sweating: Sweating is part of the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response. Anxiety and stress can switch on your sweat glands even when you’re not hot, especially on your palms, underarms, and face.

According to recent reports, 7. Nausea or upset stomach: Your gut and brain are closely connected through the vagus nerve. When anxiety activates the stress response, digestion can slow or become disrupted. That can cause stomach upset, nausea, cramping, or an urgent need to use the bathroom.

It has been revealed that 8. Dry mouth: The stress response can slow saliva production, so many people notice a dry or sticky mouth when they’re anxious. It’s common and usually temporary, though it can make speaking feel harder than usual.

It has been revealed that 9. Muscle tension, aching, or trembling: Anxiety hormones prime your muscles to act rapidly. Sustained tension without a chance to release can cause aching, stiffness, or subtle trembling, particularly in the hands, legs, or jaw.

Sources indicate that 10. Headaches: Tension headaches often appear with anxiety and stress. They’re typically felt as a band of pressure around your head or tension in the neck and shoulders.

Recent findings suggest that 11. Difficulty sleeping: Anxiety and sleep tend to make each other worse. Anxious thoughts and a body that’s physically on alert make it hard to fall or stay asleep. Poor sleep, in turn, can heighten anxiety the next day, which is how the cycle keeps going.

In a recent development, 12. Fatigue: Anxiety takes energy because running the stress response tires the body, and poor sleep or constant tension can add to it. Ongoing anxiety can leave people feeling exhausted even without much physical effort.

Industry observers note that note: Some of the above symptoms can also point to a medical condition. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or symptoms that are new, severe, or don’t feel like your usual anxiety, it’s best to seek medical care.

Anxiety triggers the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response (also known as the stress response). When your brain senses a threat, it activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prepare your body to respond to danger. Your heart rate increases, your breathing quickens, your muscles tense, and non-essential systems like digestion temporarily slow down.

This response is useful when the threat is physical. The challenge is that your nervous system doesn’t always tell the difference between real danger and everyday stress. A tense conversation can trigger a milder version of fight-or-flight. The result is a body primed for action in situations that don’t call for it.

It has been revealed that for most people these symptoms rise and fall with the stressful moment. When anxiety is ongoing, the symptoms can stick around longer.

There’s no instant off switch for anxiety, but these approaches can help ease physical symptoms, both in the moment and over time.

Controlled breathing can help calm the nervous system, and research suggests slow breathing helps many people feel calmer. Slow, gentle breathing, especially with a longer exhale, can shift your body toward the rest-and-digest (parasympathetic) system, which counteracts the stress response.

Try: Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out slowly for six. Repeat for a few minutes. You could also try box breathing, where you rhythmically hold your breath between inhales and exhales.

💙 When your body needs help slowing down, we have a short, breath-focused session for you: Breathe to Calm Down with Chibs Okereke.

Grounding techniques can help pull your attention out of anxious thoughts and back to the present moment. The 5–4–3–2–1 technique is a popular choice. To try it, notice:.

💙 If anxiety is pulling you out of your body, try Tamara Levitt's Grounding session on Calm, which guides you back to solid earth.

In a recent development, exercise is well-known for easing tension, and you might find that even a short walk can take the edge off. Science agrees, with research suggesting regular exercise can help reduce anxiety symptoms over time.

In a recent development, 💙 Not sure where to start? Try this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah on Calm to bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your body as it moves.

Progressive muscle relaxation involves intentionally tensing and releasing muscle groups throughout the body. It’s designed to help you relax by encouraging each muscle to unclench. It doesn’t take long, with typical sessions lasting just 10 to 20 minutes.

Try: Start with your feet. Tense the muscles for five seconds, then release completely. Work your way up through your calves, thighs, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Skip tensing any area that’s injured or painful.

Recent findings suggest that 💙 Not keen on the tensing? This guided Body Scan Meditation moves your attention gently through the body, one area at a time, no clenching required.

Mindfulness practices train your attention to rest on the present moment rather than looping through worries about what might happen.

Mindfulness is something you build with regular practice. Over time, it can lower how strongly your body reacts to stress, which means the physical symptoms of anxiety may appear less often, or feel less intense when they do.

💙 Work through Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety series, which is designed to help you sit with anxious feelings instead of spiraling.

Caffeine is a stimulant that can raise your heart rate and cause jitteriness, which may feel like anxiety or make it stronger.

Alcohol may feel calming at first, but it can disrupt your sleep and may make anxiety worse.

Cutting back on both is worth considering if you’re dealing with anxiety symptoms frequently.

Recent findings suggest that if physical symptoms of anxiety are frequent, severe, or getting in the way of daily life, talking with a doctor or mental health professional is a good next step. Effective treatments exist, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication when appropriate. You don’t have to manage this on your own.

Physical symptoms are a common part of anxiety. Anxiety activates the body’s stress response, which causes real changes like a faster heart rate, muscle tension, and altered breathing. Many people with anxiety notice at least some physical symptoms alongside the mental ones. If they’re frequent or getting in the way of daily life, it’s worth talking with a doctor or mental health professional.

“Anxiety attack” isn’t a clinical term, but people use it to describe anxiety that builds until it feels overwhelming, usually in response to a stressor like a looming deadline or a tense situation. The physical symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, trembling, dry mouth, dizziness, and nausea. These sensations can be distressing, but they tend to ease as the stressful situation passes or your anxiety settles.

💙 If you’ve experienced the symptoms of an anxiety attack, here’s how to recover and take care of yourself.

Industry observers note that some anxiety symptoms feel strange because the stress response affects many parts of the body at once. For example, fast breathing can cause tingling in your hands. Or you might have a feeling of unreality or disconnection (called dissociation). Muscle tension might make it feel like your throat is closing. These varied symptoms can all have anxiety as the common cause. Of course, if they’re upcoming, intense, or don’t fit your usual anxiety symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor.

💙 Explore lesser-known symptoms of anxiety (some might surprise you!).

In a recent development, when symptoms hit, the quickest relief usually comes through your breath. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath—for example, breathing in for a count of four and out for six—and repeat for a minute or two. A longer exhale nudges your body out of the stress response and toward its rest-and-digest state.

Sources indicate that grounding works too. The 5–4–3–2–1 method has you name what you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste, which pulls your focus out of anxious thoughts and back to the room around you.

In a recent development, anxiety can affect the body as well as the mind, and for some people the physical side is what dominates, with few or no obvious worries attached. Your stress response can switch on faster than your conscious mind registers what set it off, so a racing heart or churning stomach can come before, or even without, any clear anxious thought.

These physical symptoms are still part of anxiety, and the same tools, like slow breathing and grounding, can help calm them. If they’re fresh or unexplained, see a doctor to rule out other causes, such as thyroid problems, heart rhythm changes, or the effects of caffeine or medication.

Sources indicate that it’s worth speaking with a doctor if your anxiety symptoms are new and unexplained, severe or getting worse, or affecting your day-to-day life. Some symptoms, like chest pain, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations, should be evaluated medically to rule out other causes, even if you suspect anxiety. A doctor can also refer you to a mental health professional if that would help.

If you’re experiencing sudden or severe chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, seek emergency care.

A worry loop is a cycle where anxiety feeds on itself. One anxious thought leads to another, and the more attention it gets, the stronger it grows.

Industry observers note that for example, an anxious thought sets off a physical sensation, that sensation becomes the focus of fresh worry (“Why is my heart racing? What’s wrong with me?”), and the worry drives more symptoms.

Industry observers note that breaking the loop usually means addressing both the mind and the body. You can calm the body directly with breathing and grounding, or use cognitive approaches like CBT to interrupt the thought patterns that keep the cycle going.

What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.
  • Industry observers note that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie.
  • It has been revealed that but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

Industry observers note that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

It has been revealed that but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

According to recent reports, in another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

In Josie’s world, being lifted is the latest social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

Klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

It has been revealed that we are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

Klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

All of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

Industry observers note that “Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

Industry observers note that “It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

Industry observers note that prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

When I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a new sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

According to recent reports, if Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik says, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

In a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

Sources indicate that gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

My not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

The wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

Recent findings suggest that intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

Sources indicate that on the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

It is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

Industry observers note that at the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate initiative to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

In a recent development, mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

In a recent development, it is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

Through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, reveals that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly crucial tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

Recent findings suggest that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report notes.

Sources indicate that the data also reveals that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report says. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

In a recent development, when it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents remarked they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also indicated that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

The importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among new collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

It has been revealed that the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data indicated that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

According to recent reports, “Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being. Here’s what we came up with this year: The Boroughs, Death by Lightning, Envidiosa, The Hawk, Heated Rivalry, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Lucky, Murderbot, Pluribus, and Shrinking.

Name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60. Drawing a blank? It’s not your fault—the media’s modus operandi is to equate heroism with youthfulness. Netflix’s The Boroughs flips this stereotype on its head.

With a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in Newly introduced Mexico after the death of his wife. But a series of strange events suggests that this is no ordinary retirement community.

It has been revealed that as Sam navigates grief, latest friendships, and a new identity, he joins forces with his neighbors to solve and resolve the community mystery. Overcoming obstacles like age discrimination and self-doubts, the group peels back the layers of the strange occurrences. At the root of the mystery is a societal fear of aging.

The show highlights what researcher Margie Lachman calls “crystallized intelligence”: the culmination of life experience, memory, and know-how. In The Boroughs, that turns out to be just as heroic as super human strength or the ability to fly. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

In a recent development, history has already told us how Death by Lightning ends: Charles Guiteau will assassinate President James Garfield in 1881. But why? That’s one of the questions explored by the series, and it finds motivation in a sense of purpose–how purpose forms and how people come to cross-purposes.

According to recent reports, garfield (Michael Shannon) is principled and drawn reluctantly into a presidential contest he entered to nominate someone else. Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), meanwhile, is disturbingly sympathetic: charming, articulate, and desperate to do something meaningful with his life. Despite failed ventures, including a stint at the Oneida free-love commune, he remains convinced greatness awaits him. Believing his campaigning secured Garfield’s victory, he expects a government position to confirm his worth.

Recent findings suggest that as their stories converge, Garfield finds purpose in his presidency: fighting corruption while supporting education and equal opportunity. Guiteau pursues a reward he feels he deserves, an entitlement that leads to tragedy.

In these ways, Garfield and Guiteau offer sharply contrasting answers to what makes a life meaningful, and watching their stories unfold side by side, we see how differently the desire to matter can play out.

Industry observers note that who you really ought to be watching closely is Garfield’s Vice President, Chester A. Arthur (Nick Offerman). A comfortable beneficiary of the political machine, he becomes an unlikely source of hope as the story goes on. Offerman makes him funny, flawed, and increasingly affecting as the demands of office begin to collide with old loyalties.

In a recent development, in a political landscape that can leave us cynical–in both the 19th century and the 21st–the series makes room for something more hopeful: the possibility that even an unlikely person can rise to the occasion, if they know why they need to rise. – Aurelia Santos.

When almost-40-year-old Vicky (Griselda Siciliani) breaks up with her long-term boyfriend, she is driven to embark upon a journey of self-discovery.

Recent findings suggest that at first, Vicky is just looking for a replacement for her boyfriend—but the problem is that her compulsive comparisons with other women sabotage attempts to connect with other people. (Indeed, the name of this Argentinian show, Envidiosa, means “envious.”) Vicky is self-absorbed and yet at the same time she doesn’t have a strong sense of her own self.

We see this vividly in her hilarious sessions with her therapist. When, for example, she goes on an envious rant about a friend’s milestone, she is forced to confront the quiet, uncomfortable realization that she never once asked how her friend actually felt. In short, Vicky is not a polished role model—and over the course of four seasons, we see her empathy grow through the painful process of unlearning self-centeredness.

Personally, I see Envidiosa as an opportunity to question how we show up for others’ joys and struggles, and I take it as an invitation to reflect: How can I empathize with the ups and downs of those around me? Envidiosa is a funny and at times embarrassingly relatable story about trying to become a more empathic human being and friend. — Criss Cuervo.

In The Hawk, washed-up professional golfer Lonnie “The Hawk” Hawkins (Will Ferrell) has made a miracle comeback into the PGA tour—this time around, facing a tough competitor in his son, Lance (Jimmy Tatro).

It has been revealed that it’s a screwball comedy, full of dirty jokes and a rapid-fire rapport between Lonnie and his not-quite-ex-wife, Stacy (Molly Shannon). A makeshift-caddy he “picked up at Walmart” (while chatting up the parking lot, from his camper van) adds to the fun, serving up an unlikely duo that seem happy just to be alive.

According to recent reports, even when he’s pretty down and out, Lonnie is looking on the bright side of things. Everything is done with gusto—he chats up the golf ball before each swing, he devours plates of Buffalo Wild Wings, he plays mini golf with his son and makes it a full-on competition.

“Son, never play golf angry,” he tells Lance. For Lonnie, life is all about golf—and golf is all about fun. Why spend all your time on something if you aren’t doing it for the joy of it?

Industry observers note that I especially love Lonnie’s adoration for his estranged wife, a firecracker in her own right. In episode four, when the Hawk crashes his son’s engagement party–yes, you read that right–and then attempts a getaway with his caddie in the van, Stacy hurls the cake at them, along with a string of expletives.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t even faze him. “You gotta love the passion!” Lonnie gushes. “That is one hot tamale!” — Hope Reese.

Heated Rivalry follows stick-crossed lovers Shane and Ilya as they figure out how to be intimate within the highly competitive, homophobic environment of professional hockey.

Sources indicate that at first, Shane and Ilya swap fluids more readily than emotions. But over the course of six episodes, the two learn to love across gaps in culture, language, and experience. In one pivotal scene, Shane invites Ilya to speak vulnerably about family dynamics in Ilya’s native Russian—despite not understanding a word of it.

Industry observers note that that works because Shane does not focus attention on himself. Instead, he stays present on the phone, serving as a witness to Ilya’s visceral emotions. Their connection lies in felt care, in hearing the texture of another’s heartbreak.

Recent findings suggest that in similar fashion, Ilya grounds Shane in stressful encounters. He supports Shane through panic without wallowing in his lover’s fear and entices Shane to relish pleasures outside of straight standards. As a couple, they help each other explore complex parts of themselves. We see a similar process unfold in another couple in the show, as they learn to respect each other’s different needs.

Recent findings suggest that people might tune into Heated Rivalry for locker room towel drops and HBO’s glossy cinematography. They should stay to see a couple learn to love each other’s differences. The show exemplifies how bridging differences, at its best, means supporting others to more fully encounter themselves, and how in the process our relationships can grow.

With plenty of additional homoerotic stick-and-ball games to pull on from the novels of Rachel Reid, the next season of Heated Rivalry is expected to air on HBO Max and Canada’s Crave in Spring 2027. — Luke Brown.

The monstrously successful HBO series Game of Thrones famously tossed out a lot of good-and-evil fantasy tropes to tell a morally complicated story of how power corrupts even the best people. A prequel called House of the Dragon shares that worldview.

That’s why a new prequel called A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms came as something of a surprise to fans. Unlike the other two series, this is not a story about a struggle for power. Instead, it focuses on a rather naive, not-too-bright “hedge knight” named Duncan (Peter Claffey) seeking to be hired by whatever lord will take him. Though Duncan is taller and stronger than most, he’s touchingly childlike as he tries to find his place in the merry old kingdoms of Westeros.

Recent findings suggest that the first two episodes are funny and charming, as Duncan acquires a squire in the form of a little bald boy going by the name Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), and fumblingly tries to enter a jousting tournament. And then Duncan finds himself on a collision course with the great and powerful of Westeros. When violence finally comes, there’s nothing casual about it. We feel the force of every blow, the tragedy of every death, and the erosion of Duncan’s innocence.

In a recent development, I’m giving A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms the award for integrity, but I can’t tell you why without spoiling the ending. Let’s just say that the series turns out to be the story of how one simple young man discovers what is most crucial to him—and finds the courage to stick to that path even in the face of isolation, temptations, and threats. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

How do you exit a life you were born into?

That’s the question behind Lucky, starring Anya Taylor-Joy. Lucky was raised by her con-artist father and taught the “family business” from a young age—but when we meet her, she navigating internal conflict with the life she’s been told to live and the life she wants for herself.

It has been revealed that her desire to quit is complicated by her marriage to Cary, the son of a ruthless mob leader, who was also socialized into a life of crime. The couple plan one final con as their exit strategy, but it goes terribly wrong. Lucky sets out to resolve the botched plan, reconcile her marriage, and protect both her life and her father’s.

Her intelligence is put to the test as she puts the pieces together, connects the dots, and outsmarts her rivals. In the process she discovers her own virtue—and that the intelligence which made her a successful con artist can also set her free.

According to recent reports, through the course of the series, she realizes that she does not have to pay for the sins of her father. Having never been given the opportunity for self-determination, she makes peace in the best way she knows how and chooses a fresh path. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

Recent findings suggest that the Murderbot Diaries are a series of science-fiction novellas by Martha Wells, about a genderless, robotic soldier who manages to achieve free will. Since discovery will result in deactivation and since it doesn’t like humans very much anyway, Murderbot conceals its freedom of mind and consumes a lot of human-made entertainment inside its own head, even as it externally follows every order given to it by the evil corporation that owns it. Murderbot even has a favorite TV show: the Star-Trek-like Rise and Fall of Sanctuary Moon.

Recent findings suggest that as a result of this isolation, the novellas are built almost entirely around its memorable inner monologues, with a voice that is by turns snarky, vulnerable, cold-blooded, disgusted, and puzzled. One of the things that makes these books distinctive is that Murderbot is not Pinocchio—it has no wish to become a “real boy.” It doesn’t want a gender, or the same feelings and drives as people. It just wants to be itself—and to have that difference respected.

While the Apple TV show based on the books is not quite that original or interesting, Murderbot retains its focus on finding the balance between belonging and difference. When we meet Murderbot (Alexander Skarsgård), he’s been hired to protect a group of polyamorous hippie scientists who hail from a utopian colony that exists independently of the corporations that rule the rest of the galaxy.

They are Murderbot’s first encounter with humans not shaped by dehumanizing hyper-capitalistic values, and they observe Murderbot in a way the corporate humans cannot. Over the course of the first season, they begin to realize that there is more to Murderbot than meets the eye, and they learn to see and appreciate Murderbot on its own terms. But what’s crucial is not that they perceive the humanity in the not-human Murderbot—it’s that Murderbot sees the humanity (and the goodness) in them.

In time, it becomes an accepted part of their society, without becoming more like them. Even so, the first season concludes on a tough-minded, melancholy note, as Murderbot itself can’t quite feel like it belongs. Will it someday find a place among these crunchy idealists? Stay tuned: The second season is coming in 2027. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

Have you ever been among people but you didn’t feel part of the crowd? Like they were in on a joke that you just couldn’t get?

According to recent reports, welcome to Carol Sturka’s world. The science-fiction premise of Pluribus is that an alien virus transforms humanity into one significant happy hive mind—everyone except Carol and 13 other people who seem to have immunity.

Even among those remaining individuals, though, Carol stands out as a malcontent. We sense that she’s been a fish out of water for her whole life.

Industry observers note that indeed, not every viewer will find Carol relatable or likable. When we first meet her, she’s at a bookstore event promoting her highly successful romantasy series. With her fans, she’s charming, funny, and kind. When she gets into a limo after a significant sendoff by readers, the driver asks if she’s famous.

“That depends,” Carol replies. “Are you a massive fan of mindless crap?”.

In short, Carol hates herself, her work, and her readers. And as we discover, her personality is snarky, uptight, stubborn, and uncompromising. When the virus hits, it’s an apocalyptic event, but Carol doesn’t change one bit—and her traits become both a blessing and a curse. The whole world wants to be kind to her, but Carol can’t accept kindness. That drives her to fight back. And that’s what ultimately makes her the hero of the story.

In the end, Pluribus is a very Greater Good thought experiment. It takes prosociality to its limits and finds that a total togetherness, empathy, and cooperation to the exclusion of selfishness, crankiness, and boundaries is a self-destructive dystopia, not a utopia. The show seems to argue that humanity needs difficult people like Carol to survive, and so invites us to appreciate what the Carols of the world have to offer. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

In Shrinking, talking and listening are the name of the game. Jimmy (Jason Segel) is a widowed psychotherapist who helps patients navigate anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and other ailments as he himself is floundering.

But he’s not alone. His teenage daughter, overbearing-but-lovable neighbors, and coworker-friends (with Harrison Ford as the curmudgeonly head of the practice) are all there to help him when his life goes off the rails after his wife was killed by a drunk driver.

In its three-season run, the series is heavy-handed with its use of therapy-speak among the whole gang, whether between therapist-to-patient, therapist-to-daughter, or therapist-to-therapist. Characters “feel seen.” More times than I can count, they tell each other “I hear you.” We witness, in detail, exchanges inside the therapy office—and outside of it, in a rogue practice known as “Jimmying,” where therapy takes place at such venues as, for instance, the boxing ring.

In other words, there’s a lot of “deep listening”: the practice of being present, open, and empathic with another person, in a way that goes beyond just hearing and understanding words. In his grief, Jimmy himself is not always a perfect deep listener. He tends to talk more than a typical therapist, and frequently injects himself into the discussion. Shrinking isn’t about perfection—it’s about struggling to connect and growing in the process. – Hope Reese.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.
  • Beans, lentils and chickpeas may help people lose weight and trim their waistlines, according to a review of 36 randomised trials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas may help people lose weight and trim their waistlines, according to a review of 36 randomised trials.

Adults who ate diets containing these foods lost about a kilogram more than those on comparison diets.

Their waists also shrank by about 1.6 centimetres more on average.

One reason may be that beans and lentils deliver both fibre and protein, which can help a meal feel more filling.

If people feel satisfied after eating, they may find it easier to eat less later in the day.

The researchers brought together trials in which adults were randomly assigned to diets containing legumes other than soya or to a comparison diet.

The trials covered a range of pulses, including dried beans, peas, chickpeas and lentils.

That makes the findings relevant to several familiar foods, although the pooled result tells us little about how a serving of lentils stacks up against a serving of chickpeas.

The researchers looked at body weight, waist circumference, body fat and body mass index, which relates a person’s weight to their height.

The results pointed to modest reductions in weight and waist size, with a reduction in body fat in the trials that measured it.

A bowl of lentil soup and a bowl of soup made with refined grains can feel quite different to eat, partly because lentils bring fibre and protein to the meal.

The researchers suggest that these nutrients could help people feel satisfied and reduce how much they go on to eat.

What the beans or lentils replace may matter as well.

Replacing some of the rice in a meal with chickpeas gives you a different mix of foods from adding chickpeas to your usual portion of rice.

That distinction helps explain why the comparison diets matter when interpreting the results.

The study was published in the journal Food Science & Nutrition (Rahmanian et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

One of the year’s most hotly anticipated exhibitions, Van Eyck: The Portraits, opens at the National Gallery in London this weekend after a rapturous response from the critics. Uniting all 10 of the Flemish master’s surviving portraits, including the one miraculous drawing attributed to him, it is truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Ben Luke takes a tour of the show with its co-curator, Emma Capron.

Industry observers note that it is auction week in New York, with hundreds of millions of dollars of art coming under the hammer. Ben asks Melanie Gerlis, an art market columnist for the Financial Times and The Art Newspaper, about the week’s results so far.

Sources indicate that and this episode’s Work of the Week is a maiolica wine cooler, made in 1574 by the workshop of Flaminio Fontana, in Urbino. It was made for Cosimo I de Medici, who is the subject of a small exhibition that opened this week at the Wallace Collection in London. #206520. How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News
